To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

heart rate variability (a measure of the balance between sympathetic and vagal tone) is reduced after myocardial infarct, and that the reduction is more marked in inferior than in antero-septal myocardial infarcts, and is more marked in patients with a poor than a good outcome.

heart rate variability (an indicator for the cardiac autonomic nervous system) is decreased in patients with acute myocardial infarctions (MIs) and that the decrease is more pronounced in patients with anterior than in those with inferior MIs.

heart rate variability in time domain is a sensitive parameter for early diagnosis of anterior and inferior myocardial infarctions and that the initial decrease in heart rate variability is more pronounced in patients with inferior myocardial infraction.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of the early reperfusion therapy on the cardiac autonomic nervous system in acute MI.
the time course of heart rate variability (HVR) in patients with acute myocardial infarctions (MI) undergoing early thrombolysis (TL) and delayed early coronary intervention (PTCA).
the early time course of heart rate variability in patients with acute myocardial infarctions undergoing thrombolytic therapy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HRV analysis is a useful tool to assess cardiac autonomic imbalance, but it cannot be used to predict the outcome after acute myocardial infarct.
HRV is a very useful parameter to assess autonomic balance and prognosis in patients with myocardial ischemia and infarction.
the time course of heart rate variability following MI is similar in patients with anterior or inferior myocardial infarctions and with successful or unsuccessful reperfusion therapies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the initial vagal activation in inferior MI is quickly predominated and prolonged by sympathetic activation.

the time course of HR variability after MI is characterized by an initial vagal activation, which is quickly replaced by sympathetic predominance, followed by a prolonged recovery of cardiac autonomic imbalance.
in patients with acute myocardial infarctions (MI), heart rate variability ( HRV ) is reduced in the acute phase, and this is associated with increased mortality.
The main takeaway from our work is that

we have shown for the first time in a large patient cohort that the initial vagal hyperactivation in inferior MI, as indicated by a high HRV, is quickly predominated and replaced by a sympathetic activation and that the recovery of the cardiac sympathetic-parasympathetic balance is prolonged after MI.
HRV is a sensitive and reliable measure of the autonomic imbalance after myocardial infarctions.
the early course of heart rate variability after myocardial infarct and the subsequent recovery of cardiac autonomic imbalance is independent of the success of thrombolysis and/or delayed PTCA.
